g12-physics-up1-t1.overview: Physics is the bedrock science: its laws set the stage wherever matter and energy appear. This topic maps how physics underpins chemistry, biology, geology, astronomy and modern technology — and why 'interdisciplinary' is not a buzzword but the way real discoveries happen.
objectives: Explain how physics laws constrain chemistry (thermodynamics, atomic structure)
Give examples of physics techniques used in biology and medicine
Describe the role of instrumentation in geology and astronomy
Distinguish fundamental from applied research with examples
Relate SI units and measurement to every science field
g12-physics-up1-t1.simple: One science, many faces. Chemistry is applied atomic physics; biology obeys thermodynamics; geology reads Earth through seismic waves; astronomy is physics performed at a distance. Whenever a scientist measures, models or transfers energy, physics tools are already in the room. The Ethiopian Higher Education Entrance exam loves the 'which physics principle is used in X' matching question — think energy, waves, forces.
g12-physics-up1-t1.detailed:
Physics → chemistry. The periodic table is a physics result: electron shells, quantised energy levels and the Pauli principle (all quantum mechanics) explain why elements bond and react as they do. Thermodynamics — a physics theory of heat — tells chemists which reactions release energy and which demand it. Spectroscopy identifies substances by the light they absorb or emit, a direct application of atomic physics.

Physics → biology and medicine. Vision is optics (lens + detector), echolocation is acoustics, nerve signals are electrical circuits carrying 100 m/s pulses. X-ray diffraction revealed DNA's double helix; MRI images bodies using nuclear spin in magnetic fields. Bio-mechanics applies Newton's laws to bones, joints and muscles.

Physics → Earth and space. Seismology uses wave physics to image Earth's interior without drilling. Radiometric dating uses nuclear half-lives to age rocks. Astronomy runs on gravity and spectroscopy: a star's composition, temperature, motion and distance all come from analysing its light.

Measurement as the common language. Every field borrows SI units, the scientific method, and error analysis. A biologist counting cells with a microscope and a geologist dating zircons both depend on instruments whose limits are set by optics and nuclear physics respectively.

Interdisciplinary engine. The biggest modern tools are hybrids: synchrotrons (physics machines answering chemistry and biology questions), computed tomography (X-rays + algorithms), climate models (fluid dynamics + radiation physics + chemistry). The MoE syllabus frames this as 'application of physics in other fields' — the exam expects named examples, not vague praise of science.

formulas.name: Photon energy (the chemistry bridge)
formulas.meaning: spectral lines come from quantised atomic transitions
formulas.when: any interaction of light with atoms

workedExamples.problem: A UV photon of frequency 3.0×10¹⁵ Hz breaks a chemical bond. Its energy?
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 2×10⁻¹⁸ J per photon — enough to snap typical molecular bonds, hence UV's chemical power.

workedExamples.problem: Why does carbon-14 date old wood but not million-year-old rock?
workedExamples.calculation: C-14 half-life 5 730 yr: after ~50 000 yr too little remains. Rocks need long isotopes (U-238: 4.5 billion yr).
workedExamples.answer: The method must match the timescale — physics sets the dating window.

workedExamples.problem: An echolocating bat detects an insect 5 m away. Time for the echo?
workedExamples.calculation: round trip 10 m at 340 m/s: t = 10/340 ≈ 0.029 s
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 29 ms — biology running on acoustics.

workedExamples.problem: Name the physics behind each: MRI, X-ray crystallography, GPS.
workedExamples.calculation: MRI: nuclear spin in B-fields; crystallography: wave diffraction; GPS: relativity-corrected radio timing.
workedExamples.answer: three 'other fields' transformed by three physics principles.

commonMistakes: Saying chemistry/biology are 'unrelated' sciences — their laws rest on physics
Confusing what spectroscopy measures (composition via light) with what it is not (a microscope)
Using carbon-14 for dinosaur-age samples (wrong half-life window)
Forgetting relativity corrections in GPS — real engineering depends on it
Naming the instrument instead of the principle: an X-ray machine works because of diffraction/wave physics
applications: Medical imaging: X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound
Agriculture: soil moisture probes, remote sensing by satellite spectra
Industry: flaw detection with ultrasound and X-ray radiography
g12-physics-up1-t1.summary: Physics supplies the laws, the instruments and the units that every other science runs on. Know one named example per field for the exam.

questions.q: Identifying a star's chemical composition is possible because of:
questions.explanation: Atoms absorb characteristic frequencies — spectroscopy reads composition from dark lines.

questions.q: Radiometric dating relies directly on:
questions.explanation: Half-lives are physics: nuclear decay, temperature-independent.

questions.q: MRI images the body using:
questions.explanation: Hydrogen nuclei align in a B-field; their radio signals build the image.

questions.q: The discovery of DNA's structure was powered by:
questions.explanation: Franklin's diffraction patterns revealed the helix — wave physics solving biology.

questions.q: A bat 'seeing' an insect is an example of biology using:
questions.explanation: Echo ranging = speed-of-sound × time, an acoustics calculation.

questions.q: Earth's core was inferred (never drilled) through:
questions.explanation: Shadow zones of P/S waves map the interior — wave physics as an X-ray of the planet.

questions.q: GPS positions stay accurate because engineers correct for:
questions.explanation: Satellite clocks run differently by relativity; without corrections GPS drifts ~10 km/day.

g12-physics-up1-t2.overview: Engineering is physics with constraints: budgets, materials, safety factors and humans. This topic traces how mechanics, electricity, thermodynamics and waves become bridges, power plants, telecom and the infrastructure projects reshaping Ethiopia.
objectives: Map physics principles to named engineering disciplines
Explain why engineers use safety factors
Analyse a simple structure for force balance
Connect energy conversion chains in power engineering
Cite Ethiopian engineering projects and their physics
g12-physics-up1-t2.simple: Theory meets concrete. Civil engineers apply statics (ΣF = 0, Στ = 0); electrical engineers apply circuits and electromagnetism; mechanical engineers apply thermodynamics and dynamics. The engineer's extra ingredient is doubt: real loads, real materials, real people — so designs carry safety factors of 2–10, and the physics must survive mud, heat and a decade of traffic.
g12-physics-up1-t2.detailed:
Statics of structures. A bridge deck in equilibrium satisfies ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0; trusses turn bending into pure tension/compression along members, which is why triangles dominate bridge geometry. Stress σ = F/A and strain ε = ΔL/L meet at Young's modulus E = σ/ε — steel's high E makes cables thin and strong; concrete resists compression but cracks in tension, hence rebar.

Energy engineering. A hydropower plant is a physics chain with no chemical step: potential energy mgh → kinetic → turbine torque → generator EMF (electromagnetic induction) → grid. Efficiency multiplies down the chain: 90% turbine × 95% generator ≈ 85% overall. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam converts ~5 000 MW of water power — thermodynamics and fluids wearing a hard hat.

Electrical and telecom engineering. Power grids juggle voltage to slash I²R line losses (why 400 kV transmission); electronics engineers ride the semiconductor physics of Unit 5; fibre-optic engineers use total internal reflection to carry Ethiopia's telecom backbone.

Safety factors. Ultimate strength ÷ working stress = factor of safety. Bridges use ~2–3, pressure vessels ~4, elevators ~8–12: uncertainty in loads, material defects, fatigue, corrosion and consequences of failure all inflate the number.

Thermal and mechanical design. Engines and refrigerators obey Carnot ceilings; heat exchangers and cooling towers (Ethiopian flower farms use them) are applied thermodynamics. Expansion joints on roads exist because ΔL = αLΔT is not optional.

The exam angle: given a device (pump, transformer, bridge), name the principle, the energy chain, and one efficiency loss — that three-part answer scores full marks.

workedExamples.problem: Water drops 100 m at 50 m³/s through a turbine (g = 10). Power available?
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 42–45 MW after ~85–90% turbine efficiency.

workedExamples.problem: A 10 m steel rail (α = 1.2×10⁻⁵) heats 40 °C. Expansion?
workedExamples.answer: 4.8 mm — gaps prevent buckling.

workedExamples.problem: Transmit 10 kW at 200 V vs 2 kV on a 1 Ω line. Loss each?
workedExamples.calculation: I = 50 A vs 5 A; P = I²R = 2 500 W vs 25 W.
workedExamples.answer: Stepping up 10× cuts loss 100×.

workedExamples.problem: A 20 kN cable must lift with safety factor 5; steel ultimate 500 MPa. Minimum area?
workedExamples.answer: ≥ 200 mm² (≈ 16 mm diameter).

commonMistakes: Confusing stress (Pa) with force (N)
Assuming efficiency adds instead of multiplies along a chain
Thinking high voltage itself is what's transmitted — power is constant; current is what shrinks
Ignoring torque balance when checking a beam (ΣF = 0 alone is not enough)
Using a safety factor of 1 'because the math is exact' — materials scatter
applications: Road expansion joints and rail gaps
Ethio Telecom fibre backbone (total internal reflection)
g12-physics-up1-t2.summary: Engineering = physics × constraints. Name the principle, the energy chain, and where efficiency hides.

questions.q: Trusses use triangles because they:
questions.explanation: A triangle's shape is fixed by its sides — loads go axial, avoiding weak bending.

questions.q: Power is transmitted at high voltage mainly to:
questions.explanation: P = VI fixed; higher V → lower I → loss ∝ I² falls.

questions.q: Concrete is reinforced with steel because concrete is weak in:
questions.explanation: Concrete crushes slowly but cracks under stretch; rebar takes the tension.

questions.q: A turbine gets 30 m³/s at 80 m head (g=10). Ideal power ≈:
Safety factors exist primarily because of:
questions.explanation: Real-world scatter and unknown peaks demand margin above theory.

questions.q: Two stage efficiencies 90% and 95% give overall:
questions.explanation: Multiply: 0.90 × 0.95 = 0.855, not the average.

questions.q: Expansion gaps in bridges address:
questions.explanation: Seasonal temperature swings change length; gaps absorb it.

g12-physics-up1-t3.overview: Medicine is physics wearing a white coat: sound for imaging, ionising radiation for seeing and killing tumours, magnetism and nuclear spin for MRI, lasers for surgery. This topic walks through the physics behind the machines that diagnose and treat.
objectives: Explain ultrasound pulse-echo imaging with depth = vt/2
Describe X-ray production and tissue contrast
State how CT reconstructs slices from many X-rays
Use half-life to plan radioisotope tracers
Outline radiotherapy, laser surgery and MRI principles
g12-physics-up1-t3.simple: Invisible probes, visible answers. Ultrasound sends pulses and times their echoes (tissue sound speed 1 540 m/s makes a millisecond equal ~0.77 mm of depth). X-rays stop at dense bone but cross soft tissue — the shadow is the image. Radioactive tracers glow from inside on a scanner's cameras, decaying fast enough to leave quickly. Every medical machine is one physics principle, engineered gently.
g12-physics-up1-t3.detailed:
Ultrasound. A piezoelectric crystal pulses sound above 20 kHz (typically 2–15 MHz) into the body; boundaries between tissues of different acoustic impedance reflect fractions of each pulse. Depth follows from echo delay: d = vt/2 with v = 1 540 m/s in soft tissue. Doppler ultrasound adds motion: reflected frequency shifts reveal blood-flow speed — fetal hearts and blocked arteries heard without a scalpel.

X-rays and CT. Electrons smashed into a tungsten target emit bremsstrahlung X-rays; the beam attenuates exponentially, I = I₀e^{−µx}, with µ biggest for dense, high-Z material — bone (calcium) shadows, lung (air) glows. CT rotates a thin fan beam around the patient, measuring thousands of attenuations per slice; computer reconstruction turns the set into cross-sections. Contrast: iodine dyes raise µ locally, lighting up vessels.

Nuclear medicine. Tracers like technetium-99m (T½ = 6 h) emit γ-rays detected by a gamma camera — function imaging (what organs do) versus anatomy (what they look like). Half-life planning: an 80 MBq dose after 12 h (two half-lives) is 20 MBq — enough for the scan window, gone quickly for patient safety. Radiotherapy uses the same ionising power deliberately: 6 MeV linac beams damage tumour DNA; the gamma knife converges ~200 cobalt beams so healthy tissue sees only fractions while the focus sees the sum.

MRI. Hydrogen nuclei are tiny magnets; in a strong field they align at the Larmor frequency (42.58 MHz/T — a 1.5 T scanner 'hears' 64 MHz radio). RF pulses tip them; as they relax, their emitted signals map tissue water and fat. No ionising radiation — and metal objects become dangerous missiles in the fringe field.

Lasers. Excimer laser eye surgery ablates cornea with UV precision (each pulse removes ~0.25 µm); photocoagulation seals retinal vessels; laser scalpels cauterise as they cut. Coherence + monochromaticity = focus to a micron spot.

formulas.name: Ultrasound depth
formulas.meaning: echo time converts to boundary depth

workedExamples.problem: An echo returns after 0.04 ms. Organ boundary depth?
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 3.1 cm — typical ultrasound scale: each 13 µs ≈ 1 cm.

workedExamples.problem: Tc-99m (6 h) dose calibrated at 120 MBq. Activity at scan time 4 h later?
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 76 MBq — decay math is scheduling math.

workedExamples.problem: X-ray of 100 keV loses ~half in 4 cm soft tissue. Fraction after 12 cm?
workedExamples.answer: 12.5% remains — why thicker patients need higher kVp.

workedExamples.problem: 1.5 T MRI scanner: proton resonance frequency?
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 64 MHz — FM radio band, harmless RF until gradients heat tissue.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the factor 2 in pulse-echo ranging (round trip!)
Confusing X-ray image (transmission shadow) with ultrasound image (reflection map)
Thinking radioactivity 'runs out' linearly — it halves per half-life
Believing MRI uses strong B-fields to 'pull bodies apart' — it tunes nuclear spins
Calling CT an X-ray video: it is reconstruction from many static projections
applications: Fracture and chest X-rays, cancer staging CT
g12-physics-up1-t3.summary: Sound ranges, X-rays shadow, isotopes trace, magnets align, lasers cut: five physics principles, one diagnostic toolkit.

questions.q: Ultrasound images boundaries because of:
questions.explanation: Every tissue interface reflects a small echo; timing maps depth.

questions.q: Bone appears white on a radiograph because it:
questions.explanation: Dense calcium blocks the beam, so film behind bone stays unexposed — the white shadow.

questions.q: MRI primarily images which nucleus (abundant in water)?
questions.explanation: Protons abound in body water; their spin carries the signal.

questions.q: An echo delay of 26 µs in tissue means depth ≈:
questions.explanation: d = vt/2 = 1540 × 26×10⁻⁶/2 ≈ 0.02 m = 2 cm (rule of thumb: 13 µs per cm).

questions.q: A tracer with 6 h half-life injected 12 h ago retains what fraction?
questions.explanation: Two half-lives: (1/2)² = 1/4.

questions.q: CT differs from plain X-ray by:
questions.explanation: Rotating projections + computation = cross-sections.

questions.q: The gamma knife protects healthy tissue by:
options: spreading dose over many weak intersecting beams
questions.explanation: Each path gets a fraction; only the focus receives the sum.

questions.q: Doppler ultrasound measures blood flow using:
questions.explanation: Moving reflectors shift echo frequency proportionally to flow speed.

g12-physics-up1-t4.overview: Defense systems are applied physics under hard requirements: find things at range, aim them, survive the finding. Radar, sonar, night vision, guidance — each rests on wave timing and energy transfer with little patience for imprecision.
objectives: Compute radar range from echo timing (R = ct/2)
Contrast sonar (sound in water) with radar (radio in air)
Explain stealth through shape and absorption
Apply projectile motion to ballistics
Describe IR night vision and GPS guidance physics
g12-physics-up1-t4.simple: See far, hit true. Radio pulses return from targets 300 m per microsecond — that is the whole radar ruler. Sound does the same job underwater, 1 500 m/s slow but dependable. Stealth bends reflections away and drinks what remains. Ballistics is Chapter-style projectile math with air resistance bolted on; night vision reads heat; GPS closes the loop by timing satellites.
g12-physics-up1-t4.detailed:
Radar. A transmitter fires microsecond pulses at 1–40 GHz; echoes return delayed by t = 2R/c. A 200 µs round trip puts the target at 30 km. Doppler radar subtracts motion from the shift of the echo (f_d = 2v/λ), letting weather radar see storm winds and guns' radar track shells. Pulses vs continuous-wave, antenna arrays, and chaff-style countermeasures all inherit these two facts: time and frequency.

Sonar. Radio dies in seawater (saline conducts it away), so ships ping sound: 1 500 m/s in ocean. Active sonar listens for echoes the way radar does; passive sonar just hears. The deep sound channel bends sound for thousands of km — the ocean's own waveguide.

Stealth and counter-stealth. Radar cross-section scales with shape: flat panels deflect energy off-specular, curves scatter back, and radar-absorbing carbon composites dissipate what hits them. Infrared stealth cools exhausts; low-band radar (longer λ resonant with airframe sizes) partially restores detection — the physics chase never ends.

Ballistics. A shell follows projectile equations: R = v₀²sin2θ/g in vacuum; air drag roughly halves real ranges and adds the spin of rifling for gyroscopic stability. Fire-control solutions solve it backwards: given target motion, find the aim angle — pure Newton with microchips.

Thermal and satellite guidance. Night-vision IR detectors (HgCdTe arrays) see 8–14 µm radiation that warm bodies emit over cold background. GPS guidance times four-satellite ranges and, because accuracy means metres, applies relativity corrections (satellite clocks drift ~38 µs/day, ~10 km error). A dual-use reminder: the same wave physics serves airliners and missiles — engineers carry an ethics payload too.

keyTerms.def: radio detection and ranging by echo timing
unambiguous range set by pulse spacing

formulas.name: Echo ranging
formulas.meaning: one-way distance is half the light-travel

formulas.name: Vacuum range
formulas.when: ballistics first pass; drag halves it

workedExamples.problem: Radar echo returns after 133 µs. Range?
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 20 km — rule of thumb: 6.7 µs per km.

workedExamples.problem: Sonar pulse returns from a sub in 4 s (ocean v = 1500 m/s). Distance?
workedExamples.answer: 3 km — sound's slow ruler needs patience.

workedExamples.problem: A gun fires at 800 m/s, 45°, vacuum. Range?
workedExamples.answer: 64 km ideal; drag cuts real shells toward 30 km.

workedExamples.problem: Police radar at λ = 0.032 m returns a 300 Hz upshift. Car speed?
workedExamples.calculation: v = f_d λ/2 = 300 × 0.032/2 = 4.8 m/s toward the gun.
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 4.8 m/s closing — about 17 km/h.

commonMistakes: Dropping the /2 in echo ranging (round trips!)
Expecting radar to work well underwater
Saying stealth 'absorbs all radar' — it manages cross-section, never zeroes it
Using vacuum range without noting drag roughly halves real shells
Thinking GPS ignores relativity — without clock corrections error grows ~10 km/day
g12-physics-up1-t4.summary: Time echoes (R = ct/2), read Doppler shifts, respect drag, correct clocks: defense is wave physics at demanding tolerance.

questions.q: Radar determines range primarily by:
questions.explanation: Distance lives in timing: R = ct/2.

questions.q: Sonar uses sound instead of radio because:
questions.explanation: Conductive salt water kills RF; sound carries.

questions.q: A target's closing speed appears in radar returns as:
questions.explanation: f_d = 2v/λ — motion encoded in frequency.

questions.q: Echo delay 40 µs on radar ≈ range:
Stealth shaping reduces detection by:
options: deflecting reflections away from the source
questions.explanation: Facets send energy off in useless directions.

questions.q: Rifling stabilises shells through:
questions.explanation: Angular momentum keeps the nose pointed.

questions.q: GPS needs relativistic correction because:
options: their clocks tick differently in orbit
questions.explanation: ~38 µs/day net drift = kilometres of position error.

questions.q: A sonar pings the seafloor 1.5 km deep; return time ≈:
questions.explanation: t = 2×1500/1500 = 2 s round trip.

g12-physics-up1-t5.overview: Communication is physics travelling politely: information rides electromagnetic waves, carried through copper, air and glass. This topic covers the spectrum's comms bands, modulation, fibre optics, satellites and cellular networks — the science behind an Ethiopian phone call.
objectives: Match spectrum bands to communication roles
Explain AM and FM modulation conceptually
Use total internal reflection to explain fibre capacity
Compute satellite link delays
Describe cellular reuse and EMI shielding
g12-physics-up1-t5.simple: The carrier, the message. A radio wave is a steady tone; information is what you vary about it — amplitude (AM), frequency (FM), or light intensity in a fibre. Light trapped by total internal reflection in hair-thin glass carries the world's internet; geostationary satellites stand 36 000 km up and cost you a quarter-second round trip; cellular networks reuse frequencies by shrinking the map into cells.
g12-physics-up1-t5.detailed:
Spectrum allocation. Long radio waves (kHz–MHz) diffract over hills and travel far at low data rates — broadcasting. Microwaves (GHz) punch through atmospheres in beams: radar, Wi-Fi (2.4/5 GHz), mobile backhaul, satellite up/downlinks. Infrared handles short-range links (remotes). Visible light in glass fibres is the champion: carrier ~2×10¹⁴ Hz means channel capacity measured in terabits. Higher frequency = more bandwidth, less diffraction, shorter practical range.

Modulation. AM rides the message onto amplitude — simple, noise-prone. FM rides it onto frequency — noisier bandwidth needed, immune to amplitude fades (why music and TV sound rode FM). Digital schemes key phase/amplitude combos (QAM): each symbol a small number, streaming near Shannon's channel limit. Multiplexing layers many streams: FDM (stations per frequency), TDM (time slots), WDM (colours in one fibre).

Fibre. Core n ≈ 1.48, cladding lower: rays beyond the critical angle θ_c = arcsin(n₂/n₁) ≈ 40° reflect forever. Pulses of laser light carry ~10 Gb/s each colour, 100 colours a strand, attenuation ~0.2 dB/km (95% survives 3.5 km unamplified). Ethio Telecom's backbone and the national TV fibre (ET-BG) run on this physics — plus light's immunity to electrical noise.

Satellites. Geostationary orbit: 35 784 km over the equator, matching Earth's spin, covering a third of the planet — Ethiopia's RASCOM served Africa from above. Round-trip delay: 2×36 000 km / 3×10⁵ km/s ≈ 0.24 s — audible in calls, fatal for some gaming. LEO constellations trade many satellites for milliseconds.

Cells and interference. Cellular networks divide coverage into cells; neighbours use different channels, distant cells reuse them — capacity scales with smaller cells, which is why Addis towers multiply. EMI ruins signals: coaxial cable shields, twisted pairs cancel, Faraday enclosures protect; uncontrolled, a motor's spark can wipe a radio band.

workedExamples.problem: Fibre: core n = 1.48, cladding 1.46. Critical angle inside core?
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 81° from the normal — rays skimming the wall guide; steep ones leak.

workedExamples.problem: Phone call via geostationary satellite: one-way delay?
workedExamples.answer: 0.12 s up, 0.12 s down: 0.24 s round trip — noticeable lag.

workedExamples.problem: A 60 dB loss fibre span: fraction of light arriving (0.2 dB/km)?
workedExamples.answer: A millionth — amplifiers or thinner glass needed by then.

workedExamples.problem: An FM station at 100 MHz: its wavelength?
workedExamples.answer: 3 m — antenna elements on that scale.

commonMistakes: Confusing the signal frequency (audio) with the carrier frequency (RF)
Saying AM is FM with bigger numbers (different parameter varied)
Believing fibre carries electricity
Expecting a geostationary link to feel instant (0.24 s round trip)
Thinking more towers = same spectrum everywhere (reuse needs distance)
applications: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and radio in daily devices
Undersea and national cables moving the world's data
g12-physics-up1-t5.summary: Encode on carriers, guide light in glass, bounce off orbit, reuse cells: communication is wave physics with manners.

questions.q: AM encodes information by varying the carrier's:
questions.explanation: The envelope follows the signal; FM varies frequency instead.

questions.q: Optical fibres guide light by:
questions.explanation: Beyond the critical angle, the core-cladding wall is a perfect mirror.

questions.q: Satellite phone calls feel laggy because:
questions.explanation: 72 000 km of light travel takes time.

questions.q: Cellular networks increase capacity by:
options: dividing area into cells and reusing frequencies
questions.explanation: Small cells + frequency reuse = many simultaneous calls.

questions.q: Coaxial cables resist interference because:
options: a braided shield surrounds the conductor
questions.explanation: The shield drains external fields — EMI control.

questions.q: Microwaves beat long radio for internet because they:
options: offer far more bandwidth at high frequency
questions.explanation: Higher carrier = wider usable spectrum = more data.

questions.q: λ of a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi signal ≈:
WDM multiplies fibre capacity by:
questions.explanation: Each wavelength is an independent stream in the same strand.
